item.title: @EpochAIResearch：研究显示马来西亚与中国服务器贸易数据存在巨大差异，疑涉超30亿美元英伟达AI芯片走私
item.description:
Jensen Huang’s resignation has put a spotlight on a big question: how are advanced Nvidia chips reaching China despite US export controls?

Epoch AI senior researcher Isabel Juniewicz found one clue while investigating global AI trade. Trade records are consistent with more than $3 billion of chips smuggled into China via Malaysia.

Between April 2024 and June 2025, China recorded $3.75 billion in server imports from Malaysia. However, Malaysia recorded only $0.6 billion in server exports to China.

For context, a server is a computer that goes in a data center. When servers containing AI chips cross borders, customs records them in the same category as ordinary servers.

Malaysia and China each counted about 36,000 servers shipped in that period.

But Malaysia’s records show about $17,000 per server, while China’s show about $106,000 per server. China’s per-server number is far higher than the cost of non-AI servers, which suggests the imports included AI servers.

Why the gap?

At the time, sending advanced AI chips to Malaysia was legal, but sending them on to China was not. An intermediary that shipped these chips through Malaysia to China could avoid scrutiny by declaring its exports as cheaper non-AI servers.

Chinese buyers, on the other hand, wouldn’t have broken any laws by importing these servers and would have had little reason to under-declare.

The timing stands out too. China’s server imports from Malaysia jumped from about $42 million a month to $250 million a month, starting a few months after the US banned Nvidia’s A800 and H800 chips from China in October 2023. Until then, those were the most powerful Nvidia chips that could still be legally sold to China.

Then China’s imports collapsed within weeks of Malaysia requiring permits for high-performance US AI chips leaving or passing through the country in July 2025, settling at about $50 million a month. Malaysia began requiring permits shortly after reports emerged that the US planned to restrict AI chip shipments to Malaysia.

What does it all mean?

This trade data alone does not prove smuggling.

But the pattern matches established cases where intermediaries routed restricted chips to China through Malaysia.

If these were in fact AI servers shipped from Malaysia to China, they could have held roughly the equivalent of 150,000 Nvidia H100 chips. That’s about a quarter of all AI compute smuggled to China through 2025, according to our median estimate. We don’t know how most of the remaining smuggled compute reached China.

Read the full analysis here: https://epoch.ai/data-insights/malaysia-china-chip-smuggling

To see our estimates of how much AI compute has reached China, check out our AI Chip Imports explorer: https://epoch.ai/data/ai-chip-imports

item.title: @GavinSBaker：投资人分析英伟达竞争对手正试图利用黄仁勋缺席抢占市场
item.description:
There is real fear that Nvidia might pull back on their investments and backstops. 
 
I believe this is misplaced. Nvidia’s competitors are eager to take their place, disrupt their relationships and fill any vacuum left by Nvidia.
 
There are at least three companies aggressively vying to be the new “Central Bank” of AI.
 
Across many @atreidesmgmt venture portfolio companies we are seeing Nvidia’s semiconductor and hyperscale competitors trying to lean in and displace Nvidia in important relationships. Ironically, sometimes at more favorable terms than those offered by Nvidia.
 
And of course, also beginning to see the first signs of Nvidia waking up to this risk and addressing it. Their strategic imperatives have not changed and their strategy was sound, but there is only one Jensen and competitors are now attempting to really take advantage of his absence. No one wants a monopsony at the lab layer.
 
I suspect the same thing is happening in the supply chain. But again, there is only one Jensen.

item.title: @AnthropicAI：Anthropic首席执行官达里奥·阿莫代伊就公司首次公开募股发表声明阐述愿景与安全承诺
item.description:
Remarks from Anthropic CEO @DarioAmodei on our initial public offering:

My co-founders and I started Anthropic because we believe that the most powerful technology of our time should be built for the benefit of humankind.

Daniela and I lost our father to a disease that, just a few years later, became curable. I started my career in biology, hoping to help future cures come sooner. In the lab, I saw the vast thicket of complexity that scientists face when they’re trying to understand disease and develop new treatments.

So many of the scientific tools that can cut through that thicket—tools for gene editing, gene synthesis, controlling brain cells with light—started as pure ideas. In other words, they came from thinking. From intelligence.

Human intelligence has already made diseases like plague, smallpox, and polio history for most of the world. But progress on other diseases has been too slow for so many patients and their families. Going from a great idea to a treatment can take decades: it took many years from the first discovery of a strange repeating pattern in DNA to the approval of the first treatment for a disease using CRISPR.

Nature is full of these patterns. But we’ve had too little intelligence to decipher most of them; too few scientists, with too little time. Now we can build that intelligence. Whether it’s protein folding, drug design, cancer genetics, or clinical trial administration, scientists across many areas of biology and medicine are finding Claude can help them do their research in a fraction of the time it would’ve taken just a couple of years ago. I believe sufficiently powerful AI, working in concert with humans, could compress a century of scientific and medical progress into a decade.

I don’t want to get ahead of myself. At this point all we have are early results. Experiments and clinical trials will still take time. And although they involve slow and ponderous processes, I believe those processes can be substantially accelerated by AI. We hope that in the future fewer families miss a cure by just a few years.

Medicine is just a particularly vivid example, but there are many others. Our customers—the world’s most ambitious companies, nonprofits, and individual people—are already applying the intelligence we’ve built to stimulate economic growth; lift people out of poverty; protect democracy and free societies; even make everyday services like the DMV work better. We’re proud to work alongside them. And I’m extremely optimistic about what we can do together in the future.

At the same time, we have always been honest that this technology has very real risks. These range from misuse of the technology by individuals or nation-states, to economic disruption, to losing control of AI systems. We discuss these risks not because we think they are inevitable, but because we think they are avoidable.

Avoiding them depends on the choices made by the people building AI. There is a gigantic difference between how AI will go if we pay little attention to safety, versus how it will go if we are obsessed with safety. And an obsession with safety and with public benefit has been woven into Anthropic’s DNA from the start. From safeguards against biological and cyber risks, to alignment training and testing, to looking inside our models like an X-ray, Anthropic has pioneered methods for understanding and steering the behavior of AI systems.

There is much work still to be done, and the most difficult safety work lies ahead of us. The incredible talent of the company that has enabled us to build the most capable AI systems will need to be directed, even more so than it has already, towards double- and triple-checking that those AI systems are safe and secure.
